questions.question: Define biodiversity and classification, and give three reasons why scientists classify living things.
questions.expected_answer: Biodiversity is the variety of all living things. Classification is sorting organisms into groups according to the characteristics they share. Reasons: it makes the huge variety manageable to study; it gives scientists everywhere common names so they know exactly which organism is meant; it helps identify unknown organisms; it shows relationships between organisms.

questions.question: Name the five kingdoms and give two distinguishing features and one example of each.
questions.expected_answer: Bacteria: single cell, no nucleus, cell wall; example TB bacterium or yoghurt bacteria. Protista: mostly single cells with a nucleus; example amoeba, paramecium, Plasmodium or algae. Fungi: nucleus, chitin cell walls, no chlorophyll, absorb food, made of hyphae or single cells; example mushroom, bread mould, yeast. Plants: many cells, cellulose cell walls, chlorophyll, make their own food by photosynthesis; example bean plant, yellowwood. Animals: many cells, no cell wall, no chlorophyll, eat other organisms, usually move; example earthworm, human.

questions.question: Explain why mushrooms are not classified as plants, and why viruses are not placed in any kingdom.
questions.expected_answer: Mushrooms (fungi) have no chlorophyll and cannot photosynthesise; they absorb food by digesting it outside the body; their cell walls are made of chitin, not cellulose; they store glycogen, not starch. Viruses are not cells: they are genetic material in a protein coat and can reproduce only inside living host cells, so they do not fit the cell-based features used for the kingdoms.
